title: Black Beans
summary: New World legume — backbone of Latin American, Caribbean, and Southern bowls.
origins: Native to Central and South America, black beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) were domesticated independently in Mesoamerica and the Andes. Spanish and Portuguese trade spread them across the Atlantic; they became essential in Brazilian feijoada, Cuban moros, and Louisiana red beans.
history: Archaeological evidence places bean cultivation at roughly 7,000 years old in the Americas. Enslaved Africans in the Caribbean and American South adapted black beans into rice-and-beans traditions that still define regional identity. Canned black beans only became a pantry staple in the U.S. mid-20th century.
teaching: Canned beans: rinse to cut sodium; reserve liquid for thinning sauces.
Dried beans: soak overnight or quick-soak 1 hour — never salt until tender.
One cup cooked ≈ 15g fiber — pair with rice for complete amino acid coverage.
fun_fact: Black beans are also called turtle beans — same legume, different nickname.
